ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Prior to the start of the experience sampling and mobile sensing phase, participants were asked to complete a baseline survey that consisted of demographic and Big Five personality questionnaires.
After two weeks, participants completed an endpoint survey.

Overall, participants completed 29,507 experience sampling surveys (~69 surveys per participant; 6,445 missing in total) and contributed logs of their smartphone app use (n = 12,622,401 instances of app use recorded on the foreground; n = 2,119,176 instances of social media app use; n = 1,431,199 instances of messaging app use).

Participants were asked to evaluate the extent to which four items (e.g., "I am the life of the party", "I don't talk a lot") accurately describe their behavior, using a five-point scale ranging from "Very inaccurate" (1) to "Very accurate" (5).
A depiction of the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) over four total of 465 participants completed all phases of the study from May 2019 to December 2019.
Participants were 35.3 years old on average and 65% identified as female.
Participants were recruited on Facebook and Instagram from the local metropolitan area (Columbus, Ohio, USA), and via a random survey of students from The Ohio State University.

To meet eligibility requirements, potential participants had to (a) be at least 18 years old, (b) have a US phone number, and (c) possess an Android smartphone capable of running the study application.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Prior to the start of the experience sampling and mobile sensing phase, participants were asked to complete a baseline survey that consisted of demographic and Big Five personality questionnaires.

> After two weeks, participants completed an endpoint survey.

> Overall, participants completed 29,507 experience sampling surveys (~69 surveys per participant; 6,445 missing in total) and contributed logs of their smartphone app use (n = 12,622,401 instances of app use recorded on the foreground; n = 2,119,176 instances of social media app use; n = 1,431,199 instances of messaging app use).

> Participants were asked to evaluate the extent to which four items (e.g., "I am the life of the party", "I don't talk a lot") accurately describe their behavior, using a five-point scale ranging from "Very inaccurate" (1) to "Very accurate" (5).

> A depiction of the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) over four total of 465 participants completed all phases of the study from May 2019 to December 2019.

> Participants were 35.3 years old on average and 65% identified as female.

> Participants were recruited on Facebook and Instagram from the local metropolitan area (Columbus, Ohio, USA), and via a random survey of students from The Ohio State University.

> To meet eligibility requirements, potential participants had to (a) be at least 18 years old, (b) have a US phone number, and (c) possess an Android smartphone capable of running the study application.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "Incomplete data were treated as missing at random, and statistical significance was evaluated at p < .05."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.10", "p = 0.27", "p = 0.34", "p = 0.52" ), Sentence = c("Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not find any significant association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact (social media app use: γ10 = 0.07, p = 0.10; :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 621 columns across 15 data files.
#### Issues Identified

23 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 15 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Prior to the start of the experience sampling and mobile sensing phase, participants were asked to complete a baseline survey that consisted of demographic and Big Five personality questionnaires.
After two weeks, participants completed an endpoint survey.

Overall, participants completed 29,507 experience sampling surveys (~69 surveys per participant; 6,445 missing in total) and contributed logs of their smartphone app use (n = 12,622,401 instances of app use recorded on the foreground; n = 2,119,176 instances of social media app use; n = 1,431,199 instances of messaging app use).

Participants were asked to evaluate the extent to which four items (e.g., "I am the life of the party", "I don't talk a lot") accurately describe their behavior, using a five-point scale ranging from "Very inaccurate" (1) to "Very accurate" (5).
A depiction of the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) over four total of 465 participants completed all phases of the study from May 2019 to December 2019.
Participants were 35.3 years old on average and 65% identified as female.
Participants were recruited on Facebook and Instagram from the local metropolitan area (Columbus, Ohio, USA), and via a random survey of students from The Ohio State University.

To meet eligibility requirements, potential participants had to (a) be at least 18 years old, (b) have a US phone number, and (c) possess an Android smartphone capable of running the study application.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 15 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:15, File = c("Prep (1).R", "Prep (2).R", 
"Social Media vs. Messaging 2025.Rmd", "AMPPS R Markdown FINAL.Rmd", 
"Analysis.R", "Analysis.Rmd", "interaction-quality-and-energy_revision.R", 
"LCA Analysis Final.Rmd", "LongitudinalAnalysisChapter_Code.R", 
"LongitudinalAnalysisChapter_Code.Rmd", "mHealth RMarkdown Final.Rmd", 
"Time Perception.Rmd", "Social App Use to Time Perception Redux.Rmd", 
"Time Perception Analysis.R", "Viz.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"Prep (1).R", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
"—", "—", "—", "Time Perception.Rmd", "Time Perception.Rmd", 
"—"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", "numeric", "none", 
"none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "none", 
"dependency", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -15L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**13 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `LCAdata Raw Data 10 03.csv` to `../Data/LCAdata Raw Data 10 03.csv` (in LCA Analysis Final.Rmd); `LCAdata Raw Data 10 03.csv` to `../Data/LCAdata Raw Data 10 03.csv` (in Social Media vs. Messaging 2025.Rmd); `route data DID.csv` to `../Data/route data DID.csv` (in Analysis.Rmd); `destination data DID.csv` to `../Data/destination data DID.csv` (in Analysis.Rmd); `Study1-mHealthData(5-5-22).csv` to `../Data/Study1-mHealthData(5-5-22).csv` (in mHealth RMarkdown Final.Rmd); `Study2-mHealthData(5-5-22).csv` to `../Data/Study2-mHealthData(5-5-22).csv` (in mHealth RMarkdown Final.Rmd); `mHealth Apps Self-Report Validity.csv` to `../Data/mHealth Apps Self-Report Validity.csv` (in mHealth RMarkdown Final.Rmd); `Time Perception (2-3) DID.csv` to `../Data/Time Perception (2-3) DID.csv` (in Social App Use to Time Perception Redux.Rmd); `Self-Reported Social Apps.csv` to `../Data/Self-Reported Social Apps.csv` (in Time Perception.Rmd); `~/Desktop/new life/projects/Personality_ESMdata_0808.csv` to `../../Data/Personality_ESMdata_0808.csv` (in interaction-quality-and-energy_revision.R), and 3 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 13 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `part b - ddpercent clean.csv`, `clusterids.csv`, `all app data 5 21 noel new 7 18.csv`, `baseline data (12-30).csv`, `part c - clean.csv`, `daily apps final.csv`, `data for multilevelcorr 9 29.csv`, `ids with valid log data.csv`, `all app data 8 8.csv`, `master data 1 3 pipeline.csv`, `experiencesurveys.csv`, `device_data_all_alt.csv`, `self-reported apps.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 15 scripts: 2 ran without error, 9 errored, 1 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `Prep (2).R` after `Prep (1).R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first; a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

**Undefined-variable errors**

**4 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Prep (1).R", "Prep (2).R", "Analysis.R", 
"Viz.R"), "Missing variable" = c("master", "master", "stays", 
"stays"), "Defined in" = c("(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)", 
"(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)", "Analysis.Rmd, Prep (1).R, Prep (2).R", 
"Analysis.Rmd, Prep (1).R, Prep (2).R")), row.names = c(NA, -4L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("AMPPS R Markdown FINAL.Rmd", "interaction-quality-and-energy_revision.R", 
"LongitudinalAnalysisChapter_Code.R")), row.names = c(NA, -3L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**5 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: Social App Use to Time Perception Redux.Rmd.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Social Media vs. Messaging 2025.Rmd", 
"Analysis.Rmd", "Social App Use to Time Perception Redux.Rmd", 
"Viz.R", "Time Perception Analysis.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(3L, 
1L, 1L, 1L, 2L), "Path(s) it set" = c("~/BLINDED, ~/BLINDED, ~/BLINDED", 
"~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-TheOhioStateUniversity/mCog/Papers/Post-S6 - Mobile Habits/Analysis/Data", 
"~/Desktop", "~/OneDrive - The Ohio State University/mCog/Papers/Post-S6 - Mobile Habits/Analysis/Data", 
"~/Desktop, ~/Desktop")), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

7 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**`library()` calls added**

**2 scripts use functions from packages they do not load themselves.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run them we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

info.title: An Introduction to Longitudinal Multilevel and Structural Equation Modeling Approaches for Examining Change

text.text: This chapter provides a practical introduction to two statistical frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in quantitative communication research: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling (SEM).
Focusing on intraindividual change and intraindividual variability, we illustrate how these methods can disentangle within-person processes from between-person differences.
Using real-world data, the chapter demonstrates how to model daily patterns in social interaction desires and test dynamic relationships between social app use and interpersonal needs.
Key considerations for choosing between MLM and SEM are discussed.

The chapter also highlights advanced extensions, including nonlinear growth, mediation, and multivariate models, offering researchers a foundational guide for applying these approaches to their own questions examining change.

Communication researchers study many processes that involve change, and longitudinal data and analytic techniques are essential to gain insights into changes within an individual (or other entity) over time.

In this chapter, we provide an overview and demonstration of longitudinal approaches that enable researchers to examine these within-person change processes and to make informed choices about which approaches best fit their data and research questions.
Specifically, we describe and illustrate two common techniques for modeling intraindividual change and intraindividual variability: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling (SEM).
text.formatted: Specifically, we describe and illustrate two common techniques for modeling intraindividual change and intraindividual variability: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling <ref type="bibr">(SEM)</ref>.

text.text: Using data obtained from an intensive longitudinal study, which collected experience sampling surveys in parallel with smartphone log data (N = 428), we demonstrate how these analytic approaches can provide insights into the relationship between the desire for social interaction and social app use.

Specifically, we examine (a) how individuals' desire to socially interact increases and then decreases within a day, and (b) how individuals' use of social apps impacts their desire to socially interact in "real-life".
Beyond the methods illustrated here, we also briefly discuss useful extensions of MLM and SEM.
We foresee longitudinal approaches playing an increasingly vital role in unveiling the processes that shape individuals, relationships, communities, and societies.
Change is, by definition, something that unfolds over time (Altman, Vinsel, and Brown 1981; McGrath and Kelly 1986); thus, examining change processes necessitates repeated observations over time.
text.formatted: Change is, by definition, something that unfolds over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Altman, Vinsel, and Brown 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">McGrath and Kelly 1986)</ref>; thus, examining change processes necessitates repeated observations over time.

text.text: Longitudinal data can be collected using a variety of approaches across different time scales.

For example, researchers may collect surveys over longer periods of time using panel designs, such as following the same people over months or years to study long-term changes (e.g., Coyne et al. 2020).
text.formatted: For example, researchers may collect surveys over longer periods of time using panel designs, such as following the same people over months or years to study long-term changes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Coyne et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, researchers may examine changes that occur over shorter time scales, such as tracking physiological measurements (e.g., Han, Lang, and Amon 2022), coding behaviors within a single brief social interaction (e.g., Rains and High 2021), or tracking minute-by-minute app data via "mobile sensing" (e.g., Ross et al. 2023).
text.formatted: Alternatively, researchers may examine changes that occur over shorter time scales, such as tracking physiological measurements (e.g., Han, Lang, and Amon 2022), coding behaviors within a single brief social interaction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rains and High 2021)</ref>, or tracking minute-by-minute app data via "mobile sensing" (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ross et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The defining feature of longitudinal data is not the duration of the study but rather the collection of repeated observations that can capture change in the processes of interest.
Change in communication processes comes in different forms.

Although Brinberg and Lydon-Staley (2023) provide an overview of various changes that describe communication processes, we consider two overarching ways to characterize change (Ram and Gerstorf 2009): (1) intraindividual change that pertains to enduring directional trends or shifts occurring within an individual (or entity), and (2) intraindividual variability that pertains to relatively short-term fluctuations around an equilibrium occurring within an individual (or entity).
text.formatted: Although <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brinberg and Lydon-Staley (2023)</ref> provide an overview of various changes that describe communication processes, we consider two overarching ways to characterize change <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Ram and Gerstorf 2009)</ref>: (1) intraindividual change that pertains to enduring directional trends or shifts occurring within an individual (or entity), and (2) intraindividual variability that pertains to relatively short-term fluctuations around an equilibrium occurring within an individual (or entity).

text.text: Intraindividual change is often conceptualized as directional change that manifests through trajectories of growth or decay (Ram and Gerstorf 2009).
text.formatted: Intraindividual change is often conceptualized as directional change that manifests through trajectories of growth or decay <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Ram and Gerstorf 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For example, researchers have investigated the trajectories of changes in individuals' habits of using mobile media apps, showing that habit formation tends to increase over time and then plateaus once the habit becomes established (Schnauber-Stockmann & Naab, 2019).
text.formatted: For example, researchers have investigated the trajectories of changes in individuals' habits of using mobile media apps, showing that habit formation tends to increase over time and then plateaus once the habit becomes established <ref type="bibr">(Schnauber-Stockmann & Naab, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, intraindividual variability is conceptualized as instability that manifests as fluctuations or oscillations around an equilibrium or typical level (Ram and Gerstorf 2009).
text.formatted: In contrast, intraindividual variability is conceptualized as instability that manifests as fluctuations or oscillations around an equilibrium or typical level <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Ram and Gerstorf 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For example, researchers have examined the effect of meaningful social interactions on experiences of well-being over the course of three weeks, finding that individuals' engagement in social interactions in a given week is associated with an increase in their well-being that week (Roshanaei et al. 2024).
text.formatted: For example, researchers have examined the effect of meaningful social interactions on experiences of well-being over the course of three weeks, finding that individuals' engagement in social interactions in a given week is associated with an increase in their well-being that week <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Roshanaei et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: MLM and SEM are two common frameworks that researchers can use to analyze longitudinal data and to examine intraindividual change and variability.

These frameworks are needed because repeated observations per individual (or entity) introduce dependencies within the data, and thus violate assumptions of independence that are standard in regression and analysis of variance approaches (Curran 2003; Raudenbush 2001).
text.formatted: These frameworks are needed because repeated observations per individual (or entity) introduce dependencies within the data, and thus violate assumptions of independence that are standard in regression and analysis of variance approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Raudenbush 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Both MLM and SEM accommodate this lack of independence and allow researchers to disaggregate intraindividual change/variability from interindividual differences (Curran 2003; Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).
text.formatted: Both MLM and SEM accommodate this lack of independence and allow researchers to disaggregate intraindividual change/variability from interindividual differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In the following sections, we provide details about MLMs and SEMs for examining intraindividual change and variability by outlining each approach and its assumptions.
We then discuss considerations for researchers choosing between MLM and SEM before moving on to the empirical example using experience sampling and mobile sensing data.

The observations in a longitudinal study reflect both interindividual differences (e.g., some individuals generally use social media more or less than others) and intraindividual variability (e.g., an individual uses social media more on a given day than they typically do). 1 To formally disaggregate these inter-and intra-individual components, some data management is necessary.
text.formatted: The observations in a longitudinal study reflect both interindividual differences (e.g., some individuals generally use social media more or less than others) and intraindividual variability (e.g., an individual uses social media more on a given day than they typically do). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> To formally disaggregate these inter-and intra-individual components, some data management is necessary.

text.text: Specifically, researchers must person-mean center their time-varying variables to distinguish intraindividual variability from interindividual differences.

Person-mean centering refers to calculating an individual's mean on a given repeated measures variable and subtracting that mean from the raw value of the predictor at each time point (Bolger and Laurenceau 2013; Enders and Tofighi 2007).
text.formatted: Person-mean centering refers to calculating an individual's mean on a given repeated measures variable and subtracting that mean from the raw value of the predictor at each time point <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bolger and Laurenceau 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Enders and Tofighi 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, if researchers examined the impact of recent social media app use on the desire to socially interact in daily life, they would calculate the average social media app use for each individual and subtract that mean from the amount of social media app use at each measurement occasion.

This results in two new variables for each individual: (1) a time-invariant (i.e., constant) mean of the amount of social media app use that represents the "trait" component of a given individual's social media app use, and (2) time-varying deviations of social media app use that represent the "state" component of a given individual's app usei.e., whether that individual used more or less social media at that given time point compared to their average use.

Without person-mean centering (i.e., simply using individuals' raw values), the model results would represent a conflation of the intraindividual and interindividual differences (Curran and Bauer 2011).
text.formatted: Without person-mean centering (i.e., simply using individuals' raw values), the model results would represent a conflation of the intraindividual and interindividual differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Curran and Bauer 2011)</ref>.

text.text: We recommend Enders and Tofighi (2007) for a general discussion of centering and Yaremych, Preacher, and Hedeker (2023) for a discussion of centering categorical predictor variables.
text.formatted: We recommend <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Enders and Tofighi (2007)</ref> for a general discussion of centering <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">and Yaremych, Preacher, and Hedeker (2023)</ref> for a discussion of centering categorical predictor variables.

text.text: Notably, the centering of predictor variables is more relevant to the study of intraindividual variability, rather than intraindividual change, as will become more apparent below.

In models that examine intraindividual variability, the focus is typically on how changes in one (or more) time-varying variable are associated with changes in an outcome that has been assessed repeatedly.

In these models, centering is required to disaggregate the intraindividual (state-like) component from the interindividual (trait-like) component of the time-varying variable to understand their unique impacts on the outcome variable.

In contrast, in models that examine intraindividual change (e.g., growth models), the predictor variable(s) is time, so it is common across individuals and does not need to be centered (Muthén and Curran 1997).
text.formatted: In contrast, in models that examine intraindividual change (e.g., growth models), the predictor variable(s) is time, so it is common across individuals and does not need to be centered <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Muthén and Curran 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Multilevel models (MLM), also known as hierarchical linear models or mixed-effects models, are statistical models that are commonly used for analyzing longitudinal data (Hoffman and Walters 2022; Hox, Moerbeek, and van der Schoot 2017).
text.formatted: Multilevel models (MLM), also known as hierarchical linear models or mixed-effects models, are statistical models that are commonly used for analyzing longitudinal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hoffman and Walters 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hox, Moerbeek, and van der Schoot 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Conceptually, MLMs extend the linear regression framework (Curran 2003; Heck and Thomas 2020).
text.formatted: Conceptually, MLMs extend the linear regression framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Heck and Thomas 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In simple linear regression, observations are treated as a single level due to the independent nature of individual data points.
In MLMs, observations are organized in a hierarchical structure to account for the dependencies that are introduced by the longitudinal data.

Specifically, the Level 1 "regression" equation accounts for repeated measurements within every individual over time and quantifies the association between these repeated measurements for each individual (i.e., the intraindividual association or process), while Level 2 "regression" equations account for interindividual differences by quantifying the association between individual characteristics and the intraindividual processes.
In the following sections, we (1) first describe the MLM to examine intraindividual linear change, and (2) then explain how the MLM can be modified to examine intraindividual variability.
Intraindividual change often manifests as directional trajectories, such as (non)linear growth or decline (e.g., positive linear growth, U-shaped change) over time.
These directional trajectories are commonly examined using growth curve models (Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).
text.formatted: These directional trajectories are commonly examined using growth curve models <ref type="bibr">(Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Fitting growth curve models within the MLM framework involves determining a growth trajectory for each individual in the sample and identifying interindividual differences that are associated with differences in those trajectories of change.

For example, researchers can explore the linear growth or decay in adolescents' friendship closeness by estimating their intraindividual changes in friendship closeness over the course of weeks and examining whether adolescents' social support prior to the study influences their growth trajectories in friendship over time (Pouwels et al. 2021).
text.formatted: For example, researchers can explore the linear growth or decay in adolescents' friendship closeness by estimating their intraindividual changes in friendship closeness over the course of weeks and examining whether adolescents' social support prior to the study influences their growth trajectories in friendship over time <ref type="bibr">(Pouwels et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In the MLM framework, intraindividual growth trajectories are articulated through the following Level 1 equation: where 𝑌 𝑖𝑡 is the observed outcome, Y, for individual i at measurement occasion t; 𝛽 0𝑖 represents the intercept or the value of outcome Y at the starting time point (𝑡 0 ) for individual i; 𝛽 1𝑖 represents the linear slope or the amount of change in Y for individual i between each time point; and 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 represents the residuals that account for unexplained variance in outcome Y for individual i at each time point and are assumed to be normally distributed.

Notably, the subscript i for the intercept and slope of Equation 1 reflects unique parameter estimates for each individual in the sample, and as a result, there is variability in these parameters across individuals.
In the MLM framework, the variability across these parameter estimates is captured by the random effects.

The Level 2 equations explicitly account for this variability by describing the prototypical intercept and slope across all individuals and incorporating time-invariant predictors that can further explain the underlying process of growth: where 𝛾 00 represents the prototypical intercept of the trajectory and is the grand (sample level) mean of all the intercepts across individuals; 𝛾 01 represents the association between the timeinvariant predictor Z (i.e., a stable characteristic or attribute that remains constant for each individual over the course of the study, such as race/ethnicity) and the outcome Y; and 𝑢 0𝑖 represents the deviation of individual i from the grand mean.

Likewise, 𝛾 10 represents the prototypical linear slope of the growth trajectory or the amount of change per time unit across individuals; 𝛾 11 represents how the time-invariant predictor Z moderates the slope of outcome Y; and 𝑢 1𝑖 represents the deviation of individual i from the prototypical slope.

In these equations, 𝛾 00 , 𝛾 10 , 𝛾 01 , and 𝛾 11 are referred to as fixed effects because they don't vary across individuals, and 𝑢 0𝑖 and 𝑢 1𝑖 are referred to as random effects because they do vary across individuals.
Random effects estimate intraindividual variation in the fixed effects (i.e., the prototypical intercept and slope parameters).
However, which random effects to include in the model depends on theoretical and practical considerations.

In terms of theoretical considerations, when researchers aim to investigate the heterogeneity of effects (e.g., Ross et al. 2023) or when existing literature suggests that the effects should vary between individuals, then random effects should be included.
text.formatted: In terms of theoretical considerations, when researchers aim to investigate the heterogeneity of effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ross et al. 2023)</ref> or when existing literature suggests that the effects should vary between individuals, then random effects should be included.

text.text: In terms of practical considerations, researchers should evaluate whether their sample size and power allow for including the random effects in the model (Bolger, Stadler, and Laurenceau 2011) and whether they face issues with model convergence (although the Bayesian framework is now being used to avoid convergence issues; Depaoli and Clifton 2015).

text.text: Finally, although we illustrated a growth model with linear change here, growth models are quite flexible and can be extended to describe trajectories of a variety of forms.
For instance, growth models can be adapted to model nonlinear change, including quadratic, exponential, and non-continuous (e.g., stepwise, spline) change processes.
In addition to modeling growth and decay, MLMs are also well-suited to examining intraindividual variability, which we describe next.
In addition to examining processes of intraindividual change, MLMs allow researchers to explore intraindividual variability in constructs over time.

Like the growth model, this model can incorporate time-invariant variables (e.g., trait extraversion) to account for some of the variability that exists between individuals (e.g., in their desire to socially interact) at a given point in time.

Thus, the Level 2 equations follow the form: In sum, in analyzing intraindividual variability using the MLM framework, we are interested in assessing how changes in our time-varying predictor variables are associated with changes in our time-varying outcome variable, while also considering how time-invariant variables (e.g., personality) might help explain differences in these fluctuations.
The intraindividual change and variability processes that can be tested using MLMs can also be examined using the SEM framework, which we describe next.
Structural equation modeling (SEM) is a statistical technique used to examine the relationships between manifest (i.e., observed) and latent (i.e., underlying theoretical construct) variables.
Specifically, SEM integrates factor analysis and path analysis, allowing researchers to examine both the measurement and structural components of a model.

In the following sections, we (1) describe fitting latent growth models in SEM to examine intraindividual change, and (2) introduce the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) to demonstrate how researchers can investigate intraindividual variability.

Growth trajectories can be examined in the SEM framework by using repeated observations to inform the starting point of the trajectory (i.e., the latent intercept) and the change in the trajectory (i.e., the latent slope).
Path diagrams are a common way of depicting these growth trajectories and the specified SEM.
In Figure 1, we present an exemplar linear growth model with four measurement occasions.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1</ref>, we present an exemplar linear growth model with four measurement occasions.

text.text: In the diagram, the outcome variable, Y1 to Y4, that is assessed over four occasions, is depicted as squares to indicate that it is directly observed at each time point.
These observations are reflective of the latent intercept and latent slope, depicted with circles.
The triangle represents a constant (with a value of 1 for all individuals) and is used in SEM path diagrams to depict the means of latent variables.
The single-headed arrows represent the directional link between the observed measures and the latent growth components.

The latent intercept (𝜂 𝛼 ) captures the initial status or baseline level and connects to each observed outcome equally (as represented by the path coefficients of 1) because the factor represents a constant baseline level within individuals over time.

In contrast, the model slope (𝜂 𝛽 ) represents the growth trajectory and connects the outcome variables with linearly increasing path coefficients (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3) as they mirror the passage of time across the four measurement occasions.

In this case, we have imposed a growth trajectory of positive linear change in the outcome over the study duration, but there is flexibility in what the shape of this trajectory can take (Grimm and Ram 2009; Ram and Grimm 2007).

Specifically, the measurement model, which describes the relationship between the observed indicators and the latent intercept and slope, for this linear growth model are represented as: 𝑌 𝑖𝑡 = 𝜂 𝛼 𝑖 + 𝜂 𝛽 𝑖 𝜆 𝑡 + 𝜀 𝑖𝑡 (7) where 𝑌 𝑖𝑡 is the outcome measured at time t for individual i; 𝜂 𝛼 𝑖 is the latent intercept for individual i and represents the expected level of Y for individual i at the starting point t0 (i.e., at where 𝜇 𝛼 is a vector of latent intercept means -i.e., starting points -for all individuals in the sample, and 𝜁 𝛼 𝑖 represents each individual i's deviation from the mean.
Similarly, 𝜇 𝛽 is a vector of latent slope means for all individuals in the sample, and 𝜁 𝛽 𝑖 represents each individual i's deviation from the slope.
Similar to MLM, researchers can include random effects in line with theoretical and practical considerations.
Finally, individuals' latent intercepts and slopes can covary (the latent variable covariance matrix is not depicted here).
Similar to MLM, the SEM framework can accommodate trajectories of a variety of forms (e.g., quadratic, spline).

Furthermore, although the SEM growth model (Equations 7-9) and the MLM growth model (Equations 1-3) are analytically identical (in certain situations; Curran 2003; Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016), they have some key differences in how time is incorporated into each model.

Specifically, time is the numerical predictor of the model (e.g., 𝑥 𝑡 ) in MLMs, whereas time is incorporated into SEMs through factor loadings that mirror the passage of time and are summarized in the latent slope factor (Curran and Hussong 2003).
text.formatted: Specifically, time is the numerical predictor of the model (e.g., 𝑥 𝑡 ) in MLMs, whereas time is incorporated into SEMs through factor loadings that mirror the passage of time and are summarized in the latent slope factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Curran and Hussong 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The SEM framework can also examine how a process might fluctuate within person over time.

One analytical method that captures the fluctuations of one construct and its impact on itself and another construct over time is the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman 2015; Hamaker 2023).
Specifically, the RI-CLPM describes reciprocal relationships, or directional influences, between variables measured at two or more occasions in parallel.

This model is an extension of the cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) in which observed variables at one time point are regressed on themselves (thus lagged) and each other (thus crossed) at the previous time point.
For example, researchers can use the CLPM to explore the reciprocal effect of media selection and media effects, also referred to as the reinforcing spirals model (Slater 2007).
text.formatted: For example, researchers can use the CLPM to explore the reciprocal effect of media selection and media effects, also referred to as the reinforcing spirals model <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Slater 2007</ref>).

text.text: These models suggest that individuals tend to select the media they consume based on their beliefs and behaviors, and in turn, media can reinforce their preexisting beliefs and behaviors (Slater 2007; Thomas et al. 2021).
text.formatted: These models suggest that individuals tend to select the media they consume based on their beliefs and behaviors, and in turn, media can reinforce their preexisting beliefs and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Slater 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Thomas et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: RI-CLPMs are often preferred over CLPMs because they disaggregate the trait-like portion of the variable that doesn't change over time from the state-like portion of the variable that does change over time.
In this way, they can help assess the unbiased reciprocal relationships between variables (Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman 2015). measurement occasions.
text.formatted: In this way, they can help assess the unbiased reciprocal relationships between variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman 2015)</ref>. measurement occasions.

text.text: Similar to the SEM growth model, path diagrams are helpful in understanding and representing the different components of the RI-CLPM.

In Figure 2 and in Equations 10-13, X and Y denote two distinct variables that were measured multiple (e.g., four) times with one item at each time point (although additional items can certainly be incorporated).

The RI-CLPM is composed of two components: the measurement model, which considers each observed assessment as an indicator of the latent constructs over time, and the structural component of the model, which articulates the cross-and lagged effects among these latent variables.
We begin by considering the measurement model.
Like the MLM that examines intraindividual variability, the measurement model of the RI-CLPM disaggregates the trait (time-invariant) and state (timevarying) components of our constructs of interest.

Mathematically, the measurement models are: 𝑋 𝑖𝑡 = 𝜇 𝑡 + 𝐵𝑥 𝑖 + 𝑊𝑥 𝑖𝑡 (10) 𝑌 𝑖𝑡 = 𝜋 𝑡 + 𝐵𝑦 𝑖 + 𝑊𝑦 𝑖𝑡 (11) where 𝑋 𝑖𝑡 and 𝑌 𝑖𝑡 represent the observed scores on X and Y for person i at occasion t, respectively 𝜇 𝑡 and 𝜋 𝑡 are the grand means, which are the means over all individuals, for X and Y, respectively, representing the average across all individuals at each measurement occasion t, and are depicted by the triangles in Figure 2 𝐵𝑥 𝑖 for X and 𝐵𝑦 𝑖 for Y represent the interindividual (trait-like) components of each construct and are the average value of the outcomes across time points t for individual i.
Furthermore, these parameters can be considered random intercepts as they capture an individual's time-invariant deviation from the grand means.

text.text: The  𝑥 and  𝑦 parameters capture the cross-lagged effects in the model and represent the impact of one construct on another construct over time.

For example, a positive  implies that a positive deviation from an individual's typical level of X (or Y) is associated with a positive deviation in the individual's typical level of Y (or X) at the next occasion.
Finally, 𝑢 𝑖𝑡 and 𝑣 𝑖𝑡 represent the residuals that are assumed to be normally distributed.

In sum, in analyzing intraindividual variability using the RI-CLPM, we are interested in assessing how changes in one time-varying variable are associated with changes in another time-varying variable at the following time point, after controlling for the (in)stability of the former variable.

Following our review of MLM and SEM approaches to examine intraindividual change and variability, we briefly describe a few considerations that may help researchers choose between using the MLM or SEM framework.
One of the primary distinctions between these two frameworks is their (in)ability to incorporate measurement error -i.e., the extent of unreliability in the measures.
A major advantage of SEM is that it allows for explicit modeling of measurement error.

SEMs specify latent constructs (i.e., factors) that are informed by multiple observed indicators using a measurement model, which ideally enables the separation of true score variance from random error variance in the measures and results in unbiased estimates of model parameters (Curran 2003).
text.formatted: SEMs specify latent constructs (i.e., factors) that are informed by multiple observed indicators using a measurement model, which ideally enables the separation of true score variance from random error variance in the measures and results in unbiased estimates of model parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, MLMs take the observed variables as directly representing the constructs of interest, without parsing measurement error.

Despite not considering measurement error, the use of MLM may be apt when a study design uses singleitem measures, as is often the case in experience sampling studies, because there is no measurement model to fit.
The MLM and SEM frameworks also differ in their flexibility with unbalanced data.
Repeated assessments often result in datasets with missing values and differing numbers of observations across participants.
A major advantage of MLM is its ability to accurately estimate parameters even with missing data and uneven assessment intervals across participants (Curran 2003).
text.formatted: A major advantage of MLM is its ability to accurately estimate parameters even with missing data and uneven assessment intervals across participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, SEM requires relatively balanced data (i.e., little missing data, equal intervals between measurement occasions) to correctly estimate the model (Curran 2003).
text.formatted: In contrast, SEM requires relatively balanced data (i.e., little missing data, equal intervals between measurement occasions) to correctly estimate the model <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This limitation is especially relevant in the context of experience sampling studies that come with a higher number of repeated measurements and a higher likelihood of missing data.
Balanced data may be more attainable with fewer measurement occasions.
The ability to assess model fit also differs across frameworks.
In SEM, the overall model fit is evaluated using global fit indices that assess the extent to which the estimated model fits the actual data (Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).
text.formatted: In SEM, the overall model fit is evaluated using global fit indices that assess the extent to which the estimated model fits the actual data <ref type="bibr">(Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, MLM fit assessment occurs by way of model comparison rather than through global fit indices (Barr et al. 2013).
text.formatted: In contrast, MLM fit assessment occurs by way of model comparison rather than through global fit indices <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barr et al. 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, model comparison in the MLM framework examines whether nested models (e.g., comparing a model with a random intercept to a model with a random intercept and random slope) exhibit significant improvement (i.e., decrease) in model prediction error (e.g., by examining Akaike Information one model fits better than a similar model, they do not assess whether the overall fit is good.
Finally, these two frameworks differ in terms of model specification and complexity.

SEM allows for the examination of more complex relationships among variables, such as addressing questions of longitudinal mediation (e.g., Bollen 1987) or the relation of predictors to multiple outcomes (Curran 2003).
text.formatted: SEM allows for the examination of more complex relationships among variables, such as addressing questions of longitudinal mediation (e.g., Bollen 1987) or the relation of predictors to multiple outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Curran 2003)</ref>.

text.text: While MLM cannot as easily examine mediation or multivariate outcomes, it does accommodate data with multiple levels of nesting, such as following children in a school over time across the country (i.e., time points nested within children, nested within classroom, nested within school).
In summary, considerations such as measurement error, unbalanced data, and model evaluation and complexity are critical when choosing between SEM and MLM frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data.

To help make the choice and interpretation of these models more concrete, we next illustrate how to examine intraindividual change and variability with an example from an intensive longitudinal project centered on mobile technology and daily mobility (Mao et al. 2023; Ross et al. 2023; see the OSF pagefoot_2 for more information).

text.text: We examine the relationship between social app usage and the desire to interact, as well as daily changes in the desire for social interaction.
To do so, we leverage data from Project mCog, which combined daily repeated self-report surveys with passive sensing of app log data.
Prior studies have explored the role of different types of social media and mobile phone use on individuals' social lives.

Moreover, research has shown that individuals use a variety of mobile communication channels (e.g., social media, call, text) to satisfy their need to connect with their close ties (Hall 2023; Hall and Miller 2023).
text.formatted: Moreover, research has shown that individuals use a variety of mobile communication channels (e.g., social media, call, text) to satisfy their need to connect with their close ties <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Miller 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, fewer studies have investigated the impact of mobile communication on face-to-face interpersonal interactions (e.g., Hall and Miller 2023) -or the desire to interact in-person specifically.
Therefore, we investigate the relationship between mobile social app use -specifically, social media use and messaging use -and the desire to interact in "real-life".

Before examining the impact of mobile communication on the desire for social interaction, we first explore intraindividual changes in individuals' desire to socially interact over the course of the day to better understand individuals' social interaction cycles (Warner 1988).
text.formatted: Before examining the impact of mobile communication on the desire for social interaction, we first explore intraindividual changes in individuals' desire to socially interact over the course of the day to better understand individuals' social interaction cycles <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Warner 1988</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, following Ross et al. (2023), we examined whether individuals' desire to socially interact follows a quadratic (inverted-U) trend over the course of a day.
text.formatted: Specifically, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ross et al. (2023)</ref>, we examined whether individuals' desire to socially interact follows a quadratic (inverted-U) trend over the course of a day.

text.text: In other words, we test whether an individual's desire to socially interact initially increases, peaks during the middle of the day, and then decreases toward the end of the day.
As such, our research question about intraindividual change in desire to socially interact is:
RQ1: Do intraindividual changes in individuals' desire to socially interact follow a quadratic (inverted-U) trend over the course of a day?
We next examine intraindividual variability in individuals' desire to socially interact throughout the day as a function of their social app use.
We predict that once individuals' social needs are met through social platforms, they will have a reduced desire to socially interact faceto-face.
As such, our first research hypothesis regarding intraindividual variability is:
H1: There is a negative association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact.
We further explore the moderating role of extraversion on the relationship between social app use and the desire to socially interact (Bowden-Green, Hinds, and Joinson 2020):
H2: The association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact will be weaker for individuals higher in extraversion than for individuals lower in extraversion.

We tested our hypotheses using the MLM framework due to its flexibility with unbalanced data and our use of single-item measures for our primary study variables (i.e., we cannot incorporate a measurement model and measurement error).
Prior to the start of the experience sampling and mobile sensing phase, participants were asked to complete a baseline survey that consisted of demographic and Big Five personality questionnaires.
During the following two weeks, participants used the study application to complete up to six brief surveys per day.

For each survey, participants self-reported their in vivo emotional valence, arousal level, energy level, and desire for social interaction (as well as questions tied to specific studies within the broader project).
By default, surveys were sent at random times within six equal time intervals across the day.
However, surveys could also be triggered if a participant engaged in walking (given the broader goals of the project to study daily mobility), which replaced one of the six random surveys.
These intervals were created based on the wake and sleep times that participants configured in the study application.
The study application also recorded whether the participant's smartphone screen was on or off, as well as the foreground app on the screen every (up to ten seconds).
After two weeks, participants completed an endpoint survey.
Participants who completed all parts of the study received $95.

Overall, participants completed 29,507 experience sampling surveys (~69 surveys per participant; 6,445 missing in total) and contributed logs of their smartphone app use (n = 12,622,401 instances of app use recorded on the foreground; n = 2,119,176 instances of social media app use; n = 1,431,199 instances of messaging app use).
We drew from the baseline survey to assess extraversion, from the experience sampling surveys to assess desire to interact, and from the app log data to determine social app use.
Descriptive statistics for the key study variables can be found in Table 1.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics for the key study variables can be found in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: We measured individuals' extraversion from four items collected as part of a scale measuring the Big Five personality traits -specifically, the 20-item version of the International Personality Item Pool (Donnellan et al. 2006).
text.formatted: We measured individuals' extraversion from four items collected as part of a scale measuring the Big Five personality traits -specifically, the 20-item version of the International Personality Item Pool <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Donnellan et al. 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were asked to evaluate the extent to which four items (e.g., "I am the life of the party", "I don't talk a lot") accurately describe their behavior, using a five-point scale ranging from "Very inaccurate" (1) to "Very accurate" (5).
We centered extraversion around the sample mean to facilitate interpretation.
We measured the desire to interact with one item in every experience sampling survey: "Right now, do you want to be alone or with other people?"
Participants rated their desire to socially interact on a five-point scale from "I only want to be alone" (1) to "I only want to be with other people" (5).
We focused on messaging and social media apps from our list of validated apps (for a detailed description of the app validation procedure, see Ross et al. 2023).
text.formatted: We focused on messaging and social media apps from our list of validated apps (for a detailed description of the app validation procedure, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ross et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Social media and messaging apps were largely operationalized based on the Google Play Store categories of "social" and "communication", respectively.
Based on these social media and messaging apps, we calculated binary measures of social media and messaging app use.
Specifically, app use consisted of whether a social media or messaging app was recorded in the foreground of participants' screens in the 60 minutes prior to answering an experience sampling survey.
Overall, 16,461 (58%) occasions of social media use and 15,187 (53%) occasions of messaging app use were recorded prior to a survey.

We person-mean centered individuals' social media and messaging app use to separate interindividual differences from intraindividual variability, and we included both components in our model examining intraindividual variability.
We operationalized time based on the chronological order of when the study app prompted participants to complete their experience sampling surveys each day.
As individuals received prompts six times a day, the surveys were coded from 1 to 6.

Additionally, since we speculated a quadratic (inverted-U) change in the desire to socially interact, we centered time to reduce collinearity between the linear and quadratic components of the growth model (Biesanz et al. 2004).
text.formatted: Additionally, since we speculated a quadratic (inverted-U) change in the desire to socially interact, we centered time to reduce collinearity between the linear and quadratic components of the growth model <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Biesanz et al. 2004)</ref>.

text.text: We used an MLM to examine how an individual's desire to socially interact changed over the course of a day.

For the sake of model simplicity, we only examined curvilinear changes in the desire to socially interact during the first study day for each individual (i.e., to avoid adding another level that represented the day to the MLM).

Specifically, 2,107 experience sampling surveys nested within 428 individuals were used to fit a curvilinear (U-shaped) growth model and modeled as: where 𝛽 0𝑖 represents the expected value of the desire to socially interact at the first experience sampling survey of the day for individual i; 𝛽 1𝑖 represents the expected amount of linear change in the desire to socially interact for individual i across a day; 𝛽 2𝑖 is the expected quadratic change in the desire to socially interact for individual i across a day; and residuals (𝑒 𝑖𝑡 ) account for unexplained variance in the outcome for individual i across all time points.

To account for variability in the intercept and slopes between individuals, the Level 2 equations are: where 𝛾 00 is the prototypical (i.e., grand mean) desire to socially interact for individual i at the first experience sampling survey of the day, and 𝑢 0𝑖 is the deviation of each individual i's desire to socially interact from the grand mean.

Likewise, 𝛾 10 is the prototypical linear growth in the desire to socially interact for individual i, and 𝑢 1𝑖 is the deviation of each individual i's linear slope in the desire to socially interact from the prototypical linear change.
Finally, 𝛾 20 is the prototypical quadratic change in the desire to socially interact across all individuals in the sample. 4 The random effects are assumed to be multivariate normally distributed.

text.text: We used two MLMs to examine how the fluctuations in social app (social media, messaging) use might affect individuals' desire to socially interact.

Specifically, 29,507 experience sampling surveys nested within 428 individuals were modeled at Level 1 as: where 𝐷𝑒𝑠𝑖𝑟𝑒 𝑡𝑜 𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑡 𝑖𝑡 is the reported desire to socially interact for individual i at experience sampling survey t; 𝛽 0𝑖 is the average level of an individual i's desire to socially interact; 𝛽 1𝑖 is the association between an individual i's desire to socially interact and their state social app use; and 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 are individual-specific residuals that represent the unexplained variability in an individual's desire to socially interact at each time point that is not captured by social app use and that are assumed to be normally distributed.

Interindividual differences were modeled at Level 2 as: where 𝛾 00 is the prototypical level of an individual's desire to socially interact; 𝛾 01 is the prototypical association between an individual i's trait social app use and their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 02 is the prototypical association between an individual i's extraversion and their desire to socially interact; 𝑢 0𝑖 represents the deviation of each individual i from the prototypical level of the desire to socially interact; 𝛾 10 is the prototypical effect of an individual's state social app use on their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 11 represents how individuals' trait social app use moderates the association between state social app use on their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 12 represents how extraversion moderates the association between state social app use and the desire to socially interact; and 𝑢 1𝑖 represents the deviation of each individual i from the prototypical association between state social app use and the desire to socially interact.
We included the random effects in our model to account for the heterogeneity of social media effects on individuals (e.g., Meier and Reinecke 2021).
MLM models were fit to the data in R (R Core Team 2023) using the lmer library (Bates et al. 2015).

text.text: Results from the growth model examining intraindividual changes in the desire to socially interact across a day (day 1 of sampling across all participants) are shown in Table 2.
text.formatted: Results from the growth model examining intraindividual changes in the desire to socially interact across a day (day 1 of sampling across all participants) are shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>.

text.text: As expected, the quadratic model provided the best (of the models fit) representation of the data (as indicated by the lowest AIC and BIC when compared to models with no change and linear trajectories of growth; see supplemental materials on OSF for these model comparisons).
We found that the desire to socially interact exhibited a significant inverted-U change over the course of a day ( γ20 = -0.02, p < .001).
text.formatted: We found that the desire to socially interact exhibited a significant inverted-U change over the course of a day ( γ20 = -0.02, p < .001).

text.text: Furthermore, we found significant interindividual differences in the initial level of the desire to socially interact (σ𝑢0 = 0.50, CI: [0.45, 0.56]).
In other words, individuals significantly differed in their typical inclination to socially interact at the middle of the day.

Additionally, there were interindividual differences in the linear change of the desire to socially interact (σ𝑢1 = 0.20, CI: [0.17, 0.23]), which indicates heterogeneity across individuals in the linear growth component of the desire to socially interact.
In sum, we found that the desire for social interaction shows quadratic change over the course of a day, addressing RQ1.

Our data revealed that participants' desire to engage in social interactions might be linked to circadian rhythms and daily cycles of activity and rest (Warren 1988), such that the individuals' reports of their desire to socially interact started out relatively low in the morning upon waking, steadily increased through the midday hours, peaking in the late afternoon before declining again in the evening hours leading up to typical bedtimes.

text.text: As expected, the MLM with a random intercept and slope provided the best (of the models fit) representation of the social media app use data (as indicated by the lowest AIC and BIC) when it was compared to models with no random intercept and slope.

Model fit was not different between the random intercept only and random intercept and slope models for the messaging app use model, but we  We conclude that our hypotheses (H1 and H2) were not supported: social app use in the prior 60 minutes was not associated with individuals' desire to socially interact, and extraversion did not moderate this association.
Our results suggest that social app use may not fully satisfy social needs -at least in terms of reducing motives for interacting in-person.

text.text: In this chapter, we introduced MLM and SEM frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in communication research.

Within these frameworks, we focused on capturing two major types of change processes: (1) intraindividual change, which manifests as directional growth or decay trajectories within an individual, and (2) intraindividual variability, which manifests as fluctuations around an equilibrium within an individual.

By illustrating the examination of these two change processes using an intensive longitudinal experience sampling and mobile tracking study, we hope researchers see how these models can be implemented in practice and applied to their own research questions.

There is a large range of approaches available to examine change processes (see Brinberg and Lydon-Staley 2023), and we hope this chapter serves as a springboard for researchers looking to incorporate these techniques into their own toolkits.

𝛾 00 represents the prototypical level of the outcome Y; 𝛾 10 represents the prototypical association between the time-varying predictor x and the outcome Y; 𝛾 01 represents the expected impact of the time-invariant variable Z on the outcome Y; 𝛾 11 represents how the time-invariant variable Z moderates the association between the time-varying predictor x and the outcome Y; and 𝑢 0𝑖 and 𝑢 1𝑖 represent random effects, that is, the deviation of each individual i from the prototypical level of the outcome Y and from the prototypical association between the timevarying predictor x and the outcome Y.

These models allow for variability across individuals in these parameters.

Participants were 35.3 years old on average and 65% identified as female.
Participants were recruited on Facebook and Instagram from the local metropolitan area (Columbus, Ohio, USA), and via a random survey of students from The Ohio State University.

To meet eligibility requirements, potential participants had to (a) be at least 18 years old, (b) have a US phone number, and (c) possess an Android smartphone capable of running the study application.
We excluded participants (n = 37) who did not complete at least half of the surveys and who had log data missing for at least half of the hours during the study period.
Our final sample used for analysis consisted of N = 428 participants.

We also found significant interindividual differences in the strength of the association between social app use and the desire to socially interact (social media app use: σ𝑢1 = 0.12, CI: [0.07, 0.16]; messaging app use: σ𝑢1 = 0.06, CI: [0.00, 0.11]), indicating heterogeneity in the association between social app use and the desire to socially interact among individuals in the sample.

Razieh Pourafshari (M.A., University of Tehran) is a PhD student in the School of Communication at The Ohio State University.
Her research revolves around how and when digital communication enhances or undermines feelings of connection between people.
Using intensive longitudinal methods and dyadic analysis, her work explores technology use as a dynamic, relational process operating across time, partners, and contexts.
Miriam Brinberg (PhD, Pennsylvania State University) is an Assistant Professor in the School of Communication at The Ohio State University.
Her research focuses on examining interpersonal interactions in everyday life and developing methods to better understand those interactions.

Joseph (Joe) Bayer (PhD, University of Michigan) is an Associate Professor based in the School of Communication and affiliated with the Translational Data Analytics Institute (TDAI) and Department of Psychology at The Ohio State University.
He directs the Mobile Social Cognition Lab, which combines digital trace and ecological survey methods to study the mental processes that underlie social connection.
In turn, his research grapples with how our minds are changing due to smartphone and social media habits, along with the implications for digital wellbeing and addictive behavior.
